Chapter One: How Stories Shape What We See and Ignore
Most of us like to think we make decisions based on facts and logic. We want to believe people act on what’s true and right. But, if you really look at daily life, you’ll see something different. It’s the stories we tell—about who’s good, who’s bad, what’s possible, and what isn’t—that guide our opinions and choices.
These stories aren’t just in headlines or movies. They’re hiding in jokes, in the way friends talk over dinner, even in the little things we barely notice. They’re everywhere—so common, we often don’t see them at all.
Picture this: a group of coworkers sitting around a break room table, each scrolling through their phones. Someone, clearly worn out from a tough week, sighs at a headline about yet another public figure accused of harassment. Someone else shrugs and says, “It’s just a witch hunt. People are too sensitive these days.” The rest nod, ready to move on. In that simple moment, a powerful story is reinforced: that accusations are blown out of proportion, that the real danger is to innocent men, that our world is already fair enough.
And it’s not just this one conversation. This is how whole cultures decide what’s real and what’s exaggerated. The idea of a “witch hunt” is an old myth, pulled out again and again to protect those in power. It tells us that people who speak up about injustice are just being dramatic, or even making things up. So the actual pain, the real harm, gets pushed aside.
But let’s be honest—these stories don’t just appear out of thin air. They’re built, and rebuilt, by people who benefit from them. When a famous comedian is called out for wrongdoing, the story quickly flips: “He’s a good guy. He’s always been nice to me.” Suddenly, it’s not about the harm done. It’s about the accused’s discomfort. Now, the story is focused on redemption, misunderstanding, or the dangers of overreacting.
What most people don’t realize is just how much these stories shape what’s possible. They decide who gets believed, who deserves a second chance, and who’s simply ignored. They make it easy to believe that sexism, racism, and other kinds of bigotry are just things of the past—or maybe not as bad as some people say. The myth that “things are better now” feels comforting, but really, it lets everyone dodge responsibility.
So why do these myths hang on so tightly? Well, they offer an easy way out. If the problem’s exaggerated, then you don’t have to do anything. If the real victims are actually the accused, then everyone else can just relax. It’s a story that keeps things exactly the way they are.
But every now and then, someone decides not to play along. Maybe a friend at that same table quietly asks, “But what if it’s true? What if people are finally being heard?” The room might go quiet. It’s awkward, but it’s also a crack in the story. Suddenly, it’s obvious: these stories aren’t just entertainment—they’re the rules we all live by.
Here’s something to notice. The power of a story isn’t just in what it says, but in what it helps people ignore. When the same myths are repeated over and over, they become invisible. They end up shaping laws, workplaces, even the way we see ourselves. Most of us don’t notice until someone points it out. And even then, it’s tempting to look away.
But changing the story starts with seeing it for what it is. It means noticing patterns, asking who benefits, and refusing to settle for easy answers. It’s not about being perfect, or always knowing the right thing to say. It’s about being willing to see the world as it really is—not just how it’s been described.
